title: Movie Ticket Booking
summary: Choose seats for a show, hold them while paying, and never sell the same seat twice.
problem: Design the object model of a movie ticket booking system. Theatres have screens with fixed seat layouts, and a show is one movie on one screen at one time. A user selects seats, the seats are held for a few minutes while the user pays, and the booking is confirmed only if payment succeeds. Two users must never end up with the same seat for the same show.
functional: Theatres have screens; a screen has a fixed layout of seats with a category (for example standard, premium) and per-show pricing
A show is a movie on a screen at a start time; list shows and the free seats of a show
A user selects one or more seats; the system holds all of them or none for a limited time (for example 5 minutes)
The user pays within the hold; on success the seats become booked and a booking is created; on failure or expiry the seats become free again
A user can cancel a booking before the show; the seats are released and a refund is requested
Show the price of a selection from the seat categories of that show
nonFunctional: Correctness first: no double booking even when many users click the same seat at the same moment
Bookings for different shows must not block each other
A hold that is never paid must free the seats without a person intervening
A payment gateway call can fail, time out, or succeed after the hold expired; the design must stay consistent in each case
constraints: One process is enough for the in-memory model, but state which parts would move to a database or Redis and why
Up to about 500 seats per show; many shows run at once
The payment gateway is an interface you call; you do not build it
deliverables: A class diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image) with the relationships between classes
The seat state machine (available, held, booked) and the transitions, including expiry
How all-or-nothing seat selection works and which lock or atomic operation protects it
What happens when payment succeeds after the hold has expired
The design patterns you used and where, or why you used none
Optional: code for hold, confirm and expire
hints: Availability belongs to a seat for one particular show, not to the physical seat. The same seat is free for the 9 pm show and booked for the 7 pm show.
The check that all requested seats are free and the change to held must be one atomic step per show.
A hold is a record with an owner, a set of seats and an expiry time. Expiry can be lazy (checked when read) or active (a timer sweeps), and you will probably want both.
Think about the order of operations around payment: hold, charge, confirm, and what each failure leaves behind.
reference:
This is one reasonable design. Where a decision has a reasonable alternative, it is named below.

### Classes
- `Theatre` owns `Screen`s; `Screen` owns `Seat`s (row, number, category). These are static layout data.
- `Movie` and `Show` (movie, screen, start time, price per category). `Show` is the unit of consistency: it owns the seat inventory for that show.
- `ShowSeats` (inside `Show`) maps seat id to a state: AVAILABLE, HELD (hold id, expiry) or BOOKED (booking id).
- `SeatHold` (id, user, show, seats, expiresAt, status).
- `Booking` (id, user, show, seats, amount, status: CONFIRMED, CANCELLED, payment reference).
- `BookingService` is the facade: `hold`, `confirm`, `cancel`, `expireHolds`.
- `PaymentGateway` (interface) with an adapter per provider; `PricingStrategy` (interface) so a matinee or a member discount is a new class.
- `Clock` (interface) injected so expiry can be tested without sleeping.

### Seat state machine
AVAILABLE -> HELD when a user selects the seat (only if every requested seat is AVAILABLE, or HELD with an expiry already in the past).
HELD -> BOOKED when the owner of the hold confirms with a successful payment before expiry.
HELD -> AVAILABLE when the owner releases, payment fails, or the hold expires.
BOOKED -> AVAILABLE only through cancellation.

### All-or-nothing and concurrency
`Show.tryHold` runs under a lock owned by that show (a mutex in one process, or a database row lock or conditional update in a real system): it checks that every requested seat is free, and only then marks all of them HELD. Checking and marking one seat at a time would let two overlapping requests each take part of the set. One lock per show means a popular show serialises its own bookings but never blocks other shows.

Expiry has two layers: a seat whose hold has expired is treated as available when read (lazy), and a periodic `expireHolds` sweep (or a delayed job, or a Redis key TTL) frees them and keeps the free-seat listing cheap (active).

### Payment ordering and failures
1. `hold`: seats become HELD for N minutes. Return the hold id and the expiry to the client.
2. `confirm`: re-check that the hold still exists, belongs to the user and has not expired.
3. Charge using the hold id as the idempotency key, so a retry cannot charge twice.
4. On success, call `Show.book`, which moves the seats to BOOKED only if they are still held by this hold, and create the booking.
5. On failure, release the hold.

Failure cases. Payment fails: release the hold. The charge times out with an unknown result: keep the seats held a little longer and ask the gateway for the status using the idempotency key, rather than guessing. Payment succeeds but the hold already expired and another user took the seats: refund automatically and tell the user; to make this rare, add a short grace period or extend the hold when a payment starts. The booking write fails after a successful charge: a retry with the same key is safe, and a reconciliation job compares gateway charges with bookings.

### Trade-offs and alternatives
- **Lock per show vs per seat.** One lock per show is simple and enough for hundreds of seats. Per-seat locks give more parallelism but need ordered acquisition to avoid deadlock; they rarely matter at this size.
- **Pessimistic lock vs optimistic version check.** In a database, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the show's seat rows, or a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE state = 'AVAILABLE'` that checks the affected row count, are both reasonable. Optimistic retries are cheap when conflicts are rare but wasteful for a hot release of a blockbuster.
- **Hold in memory vs in Redis vs in the database.** In memory is fine for the exercise; with several servers the hold must be shared, so Redis with a TTL, or a row with an `expires_at` column, is typical. The database as the source of truth is the safest; Redis is faster but needs care about losing holds on failover.
- **Seat status on the Seat vs per show.** A boolean on `Seat` links the 7 pm and 9 pm shows incorrectly; keep state per (show, seat).
- **Lazy vs active expiry.** Lazy alone is correct but leaves stale counts; active alone can lag and allow a short window where a seat looks held. Using both is cheap.
- **Out of scope but worth naming:** waiting rooms for very hot releases, group bookings that must be adjacent, seat maps with best-available selection, and refunds policy by time before the show.
